characters: Tuffour: an eight-year-old Ghanaian boy with short hair in a blue-and-khaki school uniform, holding a small magnifying glass.
Atiah: his eight-year-old Ghanaian girl classmate with neat cornrow braids in a blue check school uniform dress, holding an unlabelled sketchbook.
Their teacher: a kind Ghanaian female teacher in a warm terracotta-and-green fabric dress watching closely nearby.

narrationPlan.voice: A curious boy’s voice for Tuffour; a thoughtful girl’s voice for Atiah
narrationPlan.pace: Quiet and curious, like a careful search (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light, tiptoeing tune with small insect sounds (placeholder)
culturalNotes: School gardens in Ghana have many small animals. The story follows the NaCCA Science standard on organisms and why they live in particular habitats (B3.3.3.1.1).
The hunt follows a safety rule: look, do not touch, wash hands, and put everything back. Some insects bite or sting, and some are harmless.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the children are not told to touch or collect animals.
Check that the examples (worm in damp soil, frog near water, ants in a mound, bird in a tree) are right for the local area.

teacherGuide.overview: A careful bug hunt shows that animals live where they find food, water and shelter. It teaches the word habitat and respect for living things. Based on NaCCA Science standards on organisms and habitats.
learningGoals: Match an animal to its habitat.
Name two rules for watching animals safely.
beforeReading: Ask: where do you think worms, frogs and birds live?
whileReading: Pause on page 2 and ask children what the log gives the animals.
afterReading: Do a habitat chart for the school garden.
Draw one animal and its habitat.
discussion: What happens to animals when their habitat is destroyed?
reflection: How will you treat animals in your garden?

support: Match four animal picture cards to four habitat picture cards.
stretch: Compare the habitat of a frog and a fish.

culturalNotes: School gardens in Ghana have many small animals. The story follows the NaCCA Science standard on organisms and why they live in particular habitats (B3.3.3.1.1).
The hunt follows a safety rule: look, do not touch, wash hands, and put everything back. Some insects bite or sting, and some are harmless.
localiseThis: Use the animals found in your school area.
Keep hands off unknown animals; adults check the area first.
